   16: packages/auth    @respin/auth â€” Better Auth instance, requireUser/requireAdmin (THE gate,
   17:                  server layer, fail closed); middleware is an optimistic cookie redirect only
   18: packages/config  @respin/config â€” the versioned runtime config (credit costs, allowances,
   19:                  pack price, grace/pause bounds, Stripe price map); append-only versions
   20: packages/credits @respin/credits â€” the credit ledger and its ONE balance authority, the
   21:                  Stripe adapter, webhook handlers and the owner-gated billing actions
   22: ```
   23: 
   24: Rule: `app/` imports only the sanctioned surfaces â€” `respinDb` /
   25: `WorkspaceAccessError` / types from `@respin/db`, `@respin/credits/app-server`,
   26: `@respin/config/app-server` (and `@respin/config/admin-server` from
   27: `app/(admin)/**` only) â€” enforced by a default-deny lint plus a dynamic-import
   28: source scan. Every query is workspace-scoped through `withWorkspace` (tenancy
   29: T1); the balance is always `deriveBalance`, never arithmetic in a page.
   30: 
   31: ## Local dev
   32: 
   33: ```bash
   34: pnpm install
   35: docker compose up -d         # local Postgres (port 5435; see docker-compose.yml)
   36: cp env.example .env.local    # then fill values (the local DATABASE_URL is inside)
   37: DATABASE_URL=postgres://respin:respin_local_dev@localhost:5435/respin pnpm db:migrate
   38: DATABASE_URL=postgres://respin:respin_local_dev@localhost:5435/respin pnpm db:seed
   39: pnpm dev                     # `next dev` DOES read .env.local; the CLIs above do not
   40: ```
   41: 
   42: **Why the two CLI lines carry `DATABASE_URL` inline:** only Next reads
   43: `.env.local`. `db:migrate` and `db:seed` are drizzle-kit/tsx processes and see
   44: the shell's environment only â€” found by running this runbook, not by reading it
   45: (evidence run, 2026-08-17). `pnpm stripe:setup` is the exception: it loads
   46: `.env.local` itself, because the billing section below tells the operator to put
   47: the key there. **Never pipe `pnpm dev` through `head`** â€” when `head` exits the
   48: pipe closes and the dev server dies mid-session, answering a few requests and
   49: then hanging every one after.
   50: 
   51: Checks (same set CI runs): `pnpm typecheck && pnpm lint && pnpm test && pnpm db:check && pnpm build`
   52: â€” you should see all five exit 0. Tests run against in-process PGlite (R-17): no
   53: database setup needed.
   54: 
   55: The two `*.docker.test.ts` suites are the exception: they need real Postgres and
   56: LOUD-SKIP without it. They are what proves the ledger's money invariants under
   57: true concurrency, so run them too:
   58: 
   59: ```bash
   60: TEST_DATABASE_URL=postgres://respin:respin_local_dev@localhost:5435/respin pnpm test
   61: ```
   62: 
   63: Each suite creates and resets its OWN `respin_test_*` database (a name
   64: whitelist refuses anything else before connecting â€” the harness drops schema
   65: public).
   66: 
   67: ## Services (R-18: self-hosted â€” Lightsail + Postgres)
   68: 
   69: 1. **Database â€” DONE for dev**: `docker compose up -d` runs Postgres 17 on
   70:    port 5435 (container `respin-postgres`, volume `respin-pgdata`); migration
   71:    and seed are applied and verified. Production Postgres lives on/alongside
   72:    the Lightsail host â€” provisioning runbook lands with the first deploy plan.
   73: 2. **Auth â€” Better Auth, fully self-hosted (R-19)**: sessions and auth tables
   74:    live in our own Postgres; email/password works with zero third-party
   75:    accounts. Set `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` (e.g. `openssl rand -base64 32`) and
   76:    `BETTER_AUTH_URL=http://localhost:3000` in `.env.local`. You should now
   77:    see: `pnpm dev` â†’ create an account at `/sign-up` â†’ land on `/studio`
   78:    showing "<name>'s workspace" â†’ sign out returns to `/`. Google sign-in is
   79:    optional (add the OAuth client credentials; the button appears only when
   80:    configured). Admin: after signing up, copy your id from the `user` table
   81:    into `ADMIN_USER_IDS` â€” an empty allowlist denies everyone, by design.
   82: 3. **Deploy â€” Lightsail**: deploy shape (container service vs instance, TLS,
   83:    backups) is decided and documented when the first deploy is planned. The
   84:    path-scoped GitHub Actions CI (`.github/workflows/respin.yml`) is
   85:    deploy-target-independent and unchanged.
   86: 4. **Billing â€” Stripe test mode (M1)**: everything below is optional for
   87:    development â€” with no keys the app builds and runs, `/usage` and
   88:    `/settings/billing` render, and every billing control is disabled with the
   89:    remedy printed next to it instead of throwing when clicked. To exercise the
   90:    real flow (each step's **success check** is what "done" means for it):
   91: 
   92:    ```bash
   93:    # 0. A Stripe account in TEST MODE. Everything below is test data: no real
   94:    #    money moves, and test-mode cards are documented at
   95:    #    https://docs.stripe.com/testing (4242 4242 4242 4242 is the plain
   96:    #    success card).
   97:    #    Success check: the dashboard's top-left toggle reads "Test mode".
   98: 
   99:    # 0b. The Stripe CLI (needed from step 5 on, and for the evidence run):
  100:    #    winget install --id Stripe.StripeCli   # or see stripe.com/docs/stripe-cli
  101:    #    stripe login                            # interactive, opens a browser
  102:    #    Success check: `stripe --version` prints a version. On Windows, winget
  103:    #    installs it under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WinGet\Packages\ and it may
  104:    #    NOT be on a Git-Bash PATH; `stripe listen --api-key sk_test_...` works
  105:    #    without `stripe login` if you would rather not authorise the CLI.
  106: 
  107:    # 1. Test-mode secret key: dashboard â†’ Developers â†’ API keys â†’ "Secret key"
  108:    #    Put it in .env.local as STRIPE_SECRET_KEY (sk_test_...).
  109:    #    Success check: `pnpm stripe:setup` no longer prints the "not set" remedy.
  110:    #    (This script loads .env.local itself â€” it is the ONE CLI here that does.)
  111: 
  112:    # 2. Create the product + prices (idempotent â€” safe to re-run).
  113:    #    Needs DATABASE_URL too: the PACK price is created at the active
  114:    #    config's `pack.priceUsd`, because auto-top-up charges that same number
  115:    #    off-session. Re-running this IS the check that the two still agree â€” it
  116:    #    refuses with a PRICE DIVERGENCE error naming both amounts if they drift
  117:    #    (a Stripe price amount cannot be edited, so the fix is a new price plus
  118:    #    a stripePriceMap update, and the script says so).
  119:    pnpm stripe:setup
  120:    #    Success check: it prints a JSON stripePriceMap block of price ids.
  121: 
  122:    # 3. Paste that block into /admin/config as `stripePriceMap` and save.
  123:    #    (Reach it from /admin â†’ "Runtime configuration". You need to be in
  124:    #    ADMIN_USER_IDS â€” see Services step 2 â€” or the page returns 404 by
  125:    #    design, which is also what a non-admin POST to its save action gets.)
  126:    #    Paste it INTO the document already in the
  127:    #    textarea, replacing the empty `stripePriceMap` object; the editor
  128:    #    validates the whole document.
  129:    #    Success check: the page reports "Saved as v<N>", the version history
  130:    #    lists the new version with your user id beside it, and v1 is still
  131:    #    listed unchanged â€” config is append-only, never edited.
  132:    #    Failure check (worth doing once): save deliberately broken JSON. You
  133:    #    should get field-level errors, your text still in the box, and NO new
  134:    #    version in the history.
  135: 
  136:    # 4. Customer Portal configuration â€” LOOK AT IT AND WRITE DOWN WHAT IT SAYS.
  137:    #    Dashboard â†’ Settings â†’ Billing â†’ Customer portal.
  138:    #    REQ-G08 says the cancel flow always offers pause first. We enforce that
  139:    #    on OUR cancel path (/settings/billing â†’ "Cancel subscription" shows the
  140:    #    pause offer above the way out, asserted by tests). The portal is a
  141:    #    Stripe surface: it can cancel, it has no pause feature at all
  142:    #    (BillingPortal.Configurations has `subscription_cancel` and no
  143:    #    `subscription_pause` â€” checked against stripe@22.5.0), and Stripe's own
  144:    #    emails link to it. R-22 records the decision to LEAVE CANCELLATION ON
  145:    #    with its reason; this step exists so the setting is named rather than
  146:    #    inherited from a default nobody looked at.
  147:    #    Success check: record in the ledger, from the dashboard screen â€”
  148:    #    "Cancel subscriptions: ON" (needed for evidence step 7 below), and that
  149:    #    no pause option is offered there. If cancellation is OFF, turn it on:
  150:    #    evidence step 7 cannot run without it.
  151: 
  152:    # 5. Forward webhooks to the local app (leave running in its own terminal):
  153:    stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/api/stripe/webhook
  154:    #    Success check: it prints `whsec_...` â€” put that in .env.local as
  155:    #    STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET and restart `pnpm dev`.
  156:    #    Second success check: `/settings/billing` no longer shows the
  157:    #    "Billing is not configured on this server" banner, and the subscribe
  158:    #    buttons are live rather than disabled.
  159:    ```
  160: 
  161:    The webhook endpoint verifies the Stripe signature and nothing else â€” it is
  162:    deliberately outside every auth matcher. A bad signature returns 400 and
  163:    records nothing.
  164: 
  165:    **When you create the PRODUCTION endpoint**, subscribe it to exactly these
  166:    events (`stripe listen` forwards everything locally, so a missing production
  167:    subscription cannot show up in local testing):
  168: 
  169:    ```
  170:    checkout.session.completed
  171:    checkout.session.async_payment_succeeded   # delayed payments settle HERE â€”
  172:                                               # without it a slow pack payment
  173:                                               # is taken and never credited
  174:    customer.subscription.created
  175:    customer.subscription.updated
  176:    customer.subscription.deleted
  177:    invoice.paid
  178:    invoice.payment_failed
  179:    payment_intent.succeeded                   # auto-top-up
  180:    customer.updated                           # attribution for the deletion
  181:    customer.deleted                           # cascade (REQ-A04)
  182:    ```

  184: ## Recording M1 evidence (owner, test mode)
  185: 
  186: **This checklist is the ONLY thing that can discharge M1's evidence rows.** The
  187: repo's tests prove the engineering half against constructed events; they cannot
  188: prove that a real Stripe payload has the shape those fixtures assume. Nothing
  189: below may be claimed from a passing test â€” run it, then record the result in
  190: `../docs/progress/respin-m1/ledger.md`. Engineering completion and evidence
  191: completion are separate claims (build-plan working agreement).
  192: 
  193: Prerequisites: the five setup steps above done, `pnpm dev` running, and
  194: `stripe listen --forward-to localhost:3000/api/stripe/webhook` running in its
  195: own terminal (leave it visible â€” every step below should print an event there).
  196: 
  197: 1. **Subscribe at the Creator price** from `/settings/billing` (reachable from
  198:    the header nav on any signed-in page: **Billing**). Test card
  199:    4242 4242 4242 4242, any future expiry, any CVC.
  200:    **Check (amount):** on Stripe's checkout page, **write down the amount it
  201:    says it will charge**, and confirm it matches the Creator price that
  202:    `pnpm stripe:setup` created (re-run the script â€” it prints each price id's
  203:    amount). This is the only half of the accept-when clause "a test-mode user
  204:    can subscribe at **$10**" that anything can discharge: the page deliberately
  205:    prints no tier price (Stripe is the sole authority for tier amounts â€” see
  206:    the phase-4 price-honesty entry in the ledger), so if nobody records the
  207:    number here, nobody has checked it.
  208:    **Check (credits):** `stripe listen` shows `customer.subscription.created`
  209:    and `invoice.paid`; `/usage` then shows a balance of **250** credits and one
  210:    `grant` row whose **expiry is one month after the invoice's service period
  211:    end** (not one month after today).
  212:    *(build-plan accept-when: "subscribe â†’ grant"; "see 250 credits")*
  213: 2. **Try to subscribe again** while that subscription is live.
  214:    **Check:** `/settings/billing` offers no subscribe button at all â€” only
  215:    "Manage plan and payment method in the Customer Portal". This is the UI half
  216:    of the double-billing guard.
  217: 3. **Buy an overage pack.**
  218:    **Check:** a second row appears (`pack`, **+1,000**, 12-month expiry) and the
  219:    balance is **1,250**.
  220:    *(accept-when: "buy a pack, and see the ledger reflect all of it")*
  221: 4. **Re-send a delivered event**: `stripe events resend <event_id>` for the
  222:    `invoice.paid` from step 1.
  223:    **Check:** the balance does **not** change, no second `grant` row appears,
  224:    and the app answers 200. This is the idempotency path, live.
  225: 4b. **Measure the real webhook lag â€” this run is the only place it is
  226:    observable (decision R-24).** For two or three of the events above, compare
  227:    these two timestamps. **Use these two sources and no others** â€” see the
  228:    warning below.
  229:    - The event's own `created`: `stripe events retrieve <event_id>` (the JSON
  230:      carries `created` as a Unix timestamp).
  231:    - When this app began processing it: `stripe_events.received_at`. Read it
  232:      with
  233:      `docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U respin -d respin -c "select id, type, received_at from stripe_events order by received_at desc limit 5;"`
  234:    **Do NOT use `stripe listen`'s leading per-line timestamp**: that is the
  235:    CLI's *local receipt* time, not the event's `created`, so subtracting it
  236:    measures the CLIâ†’app hop (milliseconds) and yields a number that can never
  237:    trip the threshold below â€” a check that is performed but cannot fail. (If
  238:    you prefer the CLI, `stripe listen --print-json` does carry the real
  239:    `created`.) There is also **no app log line for a successful event** â€” the
  240:    webhook only logs on a refusal or a handler error â€” so `received_at` is the
  241:    processing-side source.
  242:    **Check:** a number is written down in the ledger for each â€” not "looked
  243:    fine". `CLOCK_SKEW_MS = 60_000` is currently a *guess* doing three jobs on
  244:    the money path (write-clock guard, pause-open staleness bound, pause-close
  245:    staleness bound), and R-24 accepts it only on condition that this
  246:    measurement happens. **If any legitimate event's lag exceeds ~30s, R-24 says
  247:    split the constant** â€” the delivery-lag tolerance and the clock-skew guard
  248:    stop being the same number. R-24's second trip condition is operational
  249:    rather than numeric: **if any pause or resume in steps 5â€“6 is refused**,
  250:    that is the same tripwire firing, and it is recorded the same way.
  251:    *(accept-when: "double-delivered webhook (no double grant)")*
  252: 5. **Pause the subscription** (1 month) from `/settings/billing`.
  253:    **Check:** `/usage` shows the frozen notice with the resume date; the ledger
  254:    rows' expiry dates are unchanged on screen (the shift is applied at
  255:    derivation time); Stripe shows `pause_collection` on the subscription.
  256:    *(accept-when: "pausing freezes credits")*
  257: 6. **Resume it.**
  258:    **Check:** `/settings/billing` returns to `active`, and the credits' expiry
  259:    has moved later by the pause duration. Note the exact before/after expiry
  260:    dates in the ledger entry â€” this is the accept-when clause that says
  261:    "expiry clocks correctly shifted", and only the two dates prove it.
  262: 7. **Cancel from the Customer Portal** â€” reach it through
  263:    `/settings/billing` â†’ "Cancel subscription", which shows the pause offer
  264:    first (REQ-G08).
  265:    **Check:** the interstitial offers pause **above** the link out; the portal's
  266:    cancel confirmation says the plan runs to the end of the paid period, and
  267:    `/settings/billing` then shows **"This subscription is set to end on
  268:    &lt;date&gt;"** while still serving the paid tier. Once
  269:    `customer.subscription.deleted` arrives at that period end (or immediately,
  270:    if you cancel right away) the page reports the free tier and the subscribe
  271:    buttons come back â€” a cancelled workspace is not locked out of re-subscribing.
  272:    **Note the date the page shows**: on the API version this app pins, the
  273:    portal expresses a period-end cancellation as `cancel_at`, NOT the legacy
  274:    `cancel_at_period_end` boolean, and reading only the boolean is how the first
  275:    evidence run found the page saying nothing at all (ledger, finding 1).
  276:    *(accept-when: "cancel â†’ downgrade")*
  277: 8. **Payment-failed â†’ grace â†’ downgrade** â€” **this one needs a Stripe TEST
  278:    CLOCK, and the three obvious shortcuts do not work.** All three were tried in
  279:    the 2026-08-17 evidence run and each is a dead end, for a different reason:
  280:    - the failure-on-renewal card 4000 0000 0000 0341 is declined **at Checkout**,
  281:      so no subscription is created and no `invoice.payment_failed` ever exists;
  282:    - `stripe trigger invoice.payment_failed` mints its **own** customer, which
  283:      maps to no workspace (`refused_unknown_customer`), and the invoice it
  284:      builds is not subscription-generated, which `isSubscriptionInvoice` refuses
  285:      by design;
  286:    - `subscriptions update --billing-cycle-anchor=now` generates no invoice, so
  287:      nothing is charged and nothing fails.
  288: 
  289:    What works is a customer created **with** a test clock, then advancing the
  290:    clock past a renewal whose default payment method is
  291:    `pm_card_chargeCustomerFail`. Our Checkout creates the customer itself with
  292:    no `test_clock`, so there is no route to that through the product today â€”
  293:    doing this needs either a dev-only customer-creation path that accepts a test
  294:    clock, or waiting for a real renewal.
  295:    **Check:** `/settings/billing` shows the grace state with a deadline
  296:    `graceDays` away; past that deadline the effective tier is free.
  297:    *(accept-when: "payment-failed â†’ grace â†’ downgrade" â€” recorded PENDING in the
  298:    ledger until a test-clock route exists; do not claim it from the unit tests)*
  299: 9. **Debit refused at zero balance** â€” **not runnable at M1.** The only debit
  300:    caller is the generation pipeline, which ships at M3; the debit API and its
  301:    refusal are tested in `packages/credits`. Record this row as still pending
  302:    rather than claiming it.
  303: 
  304: Also record, plainly: whether any real payload differed from what the fixtures
  305: assume (the invoice line shape, the checkout session's subscription field, and
  306: the pack settlement events are the three that have already been wrong once).

===== docs/initial/PRD.md =====
8-**Product thesis:** A subscription web service that turns a creator's idea, reference reel, or day of footage into a script in their own voice, mapped to shots they can actually film, built on a mechanism extracted from posts that are proven to perform - and that gets measurably better for each creator as their posted results feed back in.
9-
10:**Product-language decision (carried over from Cutdown, unchanged):** The product performs policy-compliant distribution optimisation. It never promises virality, never fabricates engagement, and never produces verbatim copies of other creators' content. The trend feature's verb is **Spin**: extract the mechanism, replace the surface. This is simultaneously the compliance position and the performance position - the evidence base behind this product shows adapted mechanisms outperform copies.
11-
12----
--
14-## 1. Problem and Opportunity
15-
16:Creative fatigue, not editing workload, is the top driver of creator burnout (40% vs 31% in the 2025 Billion Dollar Boy research), and 40-50% of new creators stop posting within six months. The nightly ritual is well documented: scroll competitors, screenshot hooks, replay transitions, end with a spreadsheet and no answers. Meanwhile 85% of creators say they would use an AI agent that learns their creative style (Adobe Creators' Toolkit, 16,000 creators), but current AI usage is shallow - generic chat for brainstorming and drafts - and audiences are punishing generic AI output (enthusiasm for AI-flavoured creator content fell 60% to 26% between 2023 and 2025).
17-
18:The gap: no product holds a creator's voice, strategy, and tested performance history in one place and uses all three to turn an input (idea, trend, footage) into a filmable script that could not have been written for anyone else. Script generators are commodities. A per-creator brain with an evidence loop is not.
19-
20:This product has already been proven at n=1. The `vivian-content` skill (voice rules, framework library extracted from viral-corpus autopsies, performance log with follows-per-1k as north star) produced one creator's best-converting post to date (5.00 follows/1k against a 1.3-1.5 baseline) and, more importantly, a repeatable method: autopsy references → extract mechanisms as named frameworks → generate through the creator's voice → log results with confounders → promote rules only on evidence. This PRD generalises that method into a multi-tenant SaaS.
21-
22:Cost of inaction: the method stays a hand-run consultancy for one creator, and the compounding assets (framework library, per-creator brains) never accrue.
23-
24-## 2. Users and Jobs to Be Done
--
26-**Primary - the solo short-form creator.** 1k-500k followers, posts 3-7 times a week on TikTok/Reels/Shorts, films and edits on their phone, no team. **Launch wedge (R-11): YouTube Shorts creators first** - trend data is available and compliant there on day one, incumbents (Spotter, vidIQ, 1of10) have proven willingness to pay for ideation on that platform, and none of them outputs a filmable script in the creator's voice. TikTok/IG-native creators are the expansion segment, entered via licensed data once pilot demand names the platform. When they open the app with an idea, a trending reel, or a camera roll of clips, they want to leave 10 minutes later with a script in their voice, hooks to test, and a shot list - not a chat transcript. Emotional job: stop dreading the blank page; stop feeling like their output could have been posted by anyone.
27-
28:**Secondary - the creator-operator (Studio tier).** A creator with a VA/editor, or a micro-agency running 2-5 creator accounts. Needs separate creator brains per account, seats, and no leakage of voice or performance data between profiles.
29-
30-**Internal - the curator.** Maintains the shared framework library: approves new frameworks proposed from autopsies, marks saturation, retires stale entries. Day one this is the founder; the admin surface must exist from the start because the library is the compounding asset.
--
38-**The three layers (the core IP):**
39-
40:1. **Universal laws** - a small set of evidence-backed rules applied to every generation: identity converts followers while advice buys views; reach and conversion are separate levers and every output names which it pulls; open threads beat resolved endings; and the anti-AI-slop voice rules (no fragment triads, no antithesis constructions, no invented personal details - placeholders marked `[check]` instead). These rules exist because they measurably separate output from generic AI content.
41:2. **The shared framework library** - named mechanisms (Confession Arc, Self-Inventory, Borrowed Concept, Quest Pilot...) extracted from autopsies of high-performing posts. Each framework is a versioned record: beats, why it converts, evidence, confidence, tested caveats, saturation status. Grown continuously by the trend monitor and by creator-run autopsies; curated by a human before anything becomes recommendable. This is Cutdown's REQ-035 contextual rule engine and REQ-070-077 trend schema, repurposed.
42:3. **The per-creator brain** - four versioned documents per creator profile: VoiceProfile (register, banned words, learned from feedback), StrategyProfile (positioning line, declared goals, content pillars, how goals bias hook/framework choice), PerformanceLog (declared north-star metric, results with confounders, promotion rules), and a personal KillTest (universal checks plus rules learned from this creator's own rejections and results).
43-
44-**The four surfaces:**
45-
46-1. **Studio** - the generation workspace. Seven modes (see REQ-030s), each producing a structured output: thesis, framework, 3-5 hooks with mechanic labels, timestamped VO script with the turn marked, shot map, on-screen text plan, caption, and an honest "why this performs" including the concept's weakest point.
47:2. **Trends** - the monitor. A feed of outperforming posts in the creator's tracked niches, each already autopsied (hook mechanic, structure, ending, follow trigger). One button: **Spin** - generate my version through my brain. Original shown alongside for reference.
48-3. **Results** - the performance log. Creator reports numbers per posted script (or connects analytics later); the system computes their normalised metric, names confounders, and proposes rule promotions the creator approves or rejects. Never silent.
49-4. **Marketing site + billing** - public site, pricing page, checkout, account/usage management.
50-
51:Why this approach over alternatives: a pure chat interface (rejected - loses the structured output and the brain), a video generator (rejected - audience backlash, commodity), a clip-repurposer (rejected - crowded, Opus/Descript own it), an analytics dashboard (rejected - tells creators what happened, not what to make).
52-
53-## 4. Functional Requirements
--
57-### A. Accounts, Workspaces, and Profiles
58-
59:**REQ-A01 [Must]:** Users sign up with email or Google, land in a personal workspace, and can create one creator profile on Free, one on Creator, one on Pro, and up to five on Studio.
60:**REQ-A02 [Must]:** Studio workspaces support up to 3 seats with roles: owner (billing + all), editor (generate + log results), viewer.
61:**REQ-A03 [Must]:** Creator profiles are strictly isolated: no voice, strategy, performance, or generation data crosses profiles or workspaces. Shared-library contributions are mechanism-level only and stripped of personal specifics (see REQ-D04).
62:**REQ-A04 [Must]:** A creator can export their full brain (all four documents plus generation history) as JSON/markdown at any time, and delete their account with full data removal within 30 days.
63-
64-### B. Onboarding - Building the Brain
65-
66:**REQ-B01 [Must]:** A guided onboarding builds a draft brain in under 20 minutes from three inputs: a structured interview (goals, positioning, north-star metric, banned words/vibes, ambitions they will say out loud), links or pasted text of 5-10 of their own past posts, and optionally 2-3 reference posts they admire. (Carried from Cutdown REQ-062.)
67:**REQ-B02 [Must]:** Every inferred brain field shows its source evidence and a confidence level, and the creator confirms or edits each before the brain activates. The system never silently infers sensitive personal traits. (REQ-061/063 carried.)
68:**REQ-B03 [Must]:** The creator declares their north-star metric at onboarding (follows/1k reach, saves/1k, link clicks, watch-through, sales) and can change it later; every subsequent output and result is judged against the declared metric, not a generic engagement score. (REQ-123 carried.)
69:**REQ-B04 [Should]:** Onboarding ends by generating the creator's first three ideas through their new brain, so the aha moment happens inside the first session.
70-
71-### C. The Studio - Generation Modes
--
82-### D. Shared Framework Library
83-
84:**REQ-D01 [Must]:** Frameworks are versioned records: name, beats, why it converts, source references, evidence entries, confidence, tested caveats, saturation status (observed/emerging/established/saturated/retired), and applicability (niche, goal type). (REQ-035 + REQ-070/076 carried.)
85:**REQ-D02 [Must]:** A named curator approves any framework before it becomes recommendable; saturated frameworks warn and demand a fresh interpretation; retired ones are not recommended. (REQ-071/073 carried.)
86:**REQ-D03 [Must]:** Any autopsy (Mode 4 or trend-monitor) that finds a mechanism not matching an existing framework can propose a new one into the curation queue.
87:**REQ-D04 [Must]:** Library contributions derived from a creator's session carry mechanism-level content only - never the creator's personal details, voice rules, numbers, or performance data.
88-**REQ-D05 [Should]:** Pro+ creators can maintain private frameworks visible only to their profile.
89-
--
93-**REQ-E02 [Must]:** Outlier scoring: a post is trending for our purposes when it outperforms its own channel's baseline (outlier ratio), not merely when it has high absolute views. Score, channel baseline, and data window are stored per item.
94-**REQ-E03 [Must]:** Each surfaced trend item is autopsied automatically: hook mechanic, structure/beats, ending style, follow/share trigger, matched framework (or new-framework proposal). Autopsies are cached; one autopsy serves all users.
95:**REQ-E04 [Must]:** **Spin**: one action generates the creator's version through their brain. A spin must change, at minimum, the subject matter, the hook wording, and one structural element; the system displays original and spin side by side and never outputs a verbatim or near-verbatim reproduction (similarity check before display).
96-**REQ-E05 [Must]:** Tracked niches per tier (Free: digest only; Creator: 1; Pro: 3; Studio: 10). Each niche produces a refreshed feed at least daily and a weekly email digest.
97-**REQ-E06 [Must]:** Every trend item shows recency and saturation; items past their window are marked stale rather than deleted. (REQ-073 carried.)
--
101-### F. Results and Learning
102-
103:**REQ-F01 [Must]:** A creator logs a result against a generated script: platform, post date, views, and the numerator of their north-star metric (follows/saves/clicks...). The system computes the normalised metric and compares against the creator's own baseline. Paid and organic are never pooled. (REQ-120/121/122 carried.)
104:**REQ-F02 [Must]:** Every result entry records confounders (topic overlap, posting-time unknown, account growth, spillover) as structured flags, and the UI never accepts a ranking claim without numbers - unverified reports are stored as unverified. (The E5 lesson, made structural.)
105:**REQ-F03 [Must]:** Learning is proposal-based: when results support a rule (framework X converts for you, hook mechanic Y underperforms), the system proposes a brain update showing sample size, effect, and confidence. Below minimum n (default 3 comparable results), findings display as exploratory and no rule is proposed. (REQ-125/126/127 carried; minimum-n discipline from the cutdown measurement program.)
106-**REQ-F04 [Must]:** Reach and conversion are reported as separate levers on every result; the product never collapses them into one score.
107-**REQ-F05 [Should]:** Optional analytics connectors (platform OAuth where APIs permit) to auto-fill results; manual entry remains the universal path.
--
109-### G. Billing, Credits, and Metering
110-
111:**REQ-G01 [Must]:** Four subscription tiers billed monthly via Stripe: Free, Creator $10, Pro $60, Studio $200 (annual with 2 months free at launch is optional). Self-serve upgrade/downgrade/cancel via Stripe Customer Portal.
112:**REQ-G02 [Must]:** A credit system meters generation. Credits are an internal unit decoupled from model tokens; every operation type has a configurable credit cost (see pricing table). Monthly credits reset on the billing anniversary; unused credits roll over one month on paid tiers, capped at one month's allowance.
113:**REQ-G03 [Must]:** When credits run out, the user can buy overage packs (default $10 per 1,000 credits, valid 12 months, consumed after monthly credits) or enable auto-top-up with a monthly spend cap they set. Generation is blocked, with a clear prompt, when balance is zero and auto-top-up is off.
114:**REQ-G04 [Must]:** The credit ledger is append-only: every debit references the generation, every credit references its source (subscription grant, pack purchase, refund, promo). Balance is derived, never stored as a mutable counter.
115:**REQ-G05 [Must]:** Credit costs per operation and monthly allowances live in versioned config changeable without deploy; an internal dashboard reports gross margin per tier (model spend vs revenue) weekly. Launch numbers below are indicative and must be tuned against real model costs before public launch.
116:**REQ-G06 [Must]:** Webhook-driven billing state: subscription created/updated/cancelled, payment failed (grace period 7 days, then downgrade to Free), pack purchased. All billing state changes are idempotent on Stripe event IDs.
117:**REQ-G07 [Should]:** Usage page: current balance, this month's burn by mode, days-to-empty estimate, invoices - plus the brain-as-asset view: brain version count, tested rules, and logged results, so the accumulating value is visible at the moment of any cancel decision.
118:**REQ-G08 [Must]:** Pause instead of cancel: any paid subscription can pause for 1-3 months (Stripe pause_collection). While paused: no charges, no monthly grants, credits frozen (expiry clocks suspended), brain and history fully preserved, read-only access. The cancel flow always offers pause first; resuming restores everything. A win-back email 7 days before pause end shows what their brain has waiting.
119-

127-| Modes | Hooks, Captions, Ideas | All 7 | All 7 | All 7 |

137-### H. Marketing Site
138-
139:**REQ-H01 [Must]:** Public site: landing page (positioning, live demo of a spin on a sample brain, pricing, FAQ), pricing page wired to checkout, terms/privacy, and a changelog. Fast, static-rendered, SEO-basic.
140:**REQ-H02 [Must]:** The landing page demo is the comparison proof: a visitor picks or types an idea and sees the same idea generated twice, side by side - generic (no brain) vs through a clearly-labelled fictional sample creator brain, with the brain's rules that shaped the output highlighted inline. This is the product's answer to "why not just ChatGPT" rendered in one screen. Zero credit cost, rate-limited by IP.
141-**REQ-H03 [Should]:** A public "framework of the week" page as content marketing, drawn from the shared library, curator-approved.
142-**REQ-H04 [Should]:** Affiliate program for creator educators: 30% recurring commission for 12 months, tracked via an off-the-shelf Stripe-native tool (Rewardful or Tolt), self-serve signup, marketing-claims policy bound by REQ-I04 (affiliates may not promise virality on the product's behalf). Ships post-launch, not launch-blocking.

153-### J. Admin and Curation
154-
155:**REQ-J01 [Must]:** Admin surface: framework curation queue (approve/edit/reject/merge), trend source management, saturation flags, user/subscription lookup, credit adjustments with reason codes, margin dashboard (REQ-G05).
156-**REQ-J02 [Should]:** Prompt/rule versioning: the assembled system context per mode is versioned, and every generation records which versions produced it, so quality regressions are diagnosable.

159-
160-1. **Activation:** % of signups that complete onboarding and generate a first script within 24h. Target 40% by day 90.
161:2. **The product's own kill test - baseline uplift:** % of active creators with ≥3 logged results where at least one system-generated post beats their own baseline on their declared metric. Target: 50% of creators with enough data by day 90. Reported with n and confounders, never as a pooled average. (Engineering completion and evidence completion are reported separately, always.)
162-3. **Conversion:** Free→paid ≥5% by day 90; logo churn on paid <8%/month.
163-4. **Unit economics:** blended gross margin on model spend ≥70% at Creator, ≥60% at Pro/Studio heavy use.
164:5. **Library growth:** curator-approved frameworks and their evidence entries per month (leading indicator of the moat).

16-| Auth | Better Auth (R-19; was Clerk) — self-hosted, sessions + auth tables in our own Postgres via its Drizzle adapter | Email/password now, Google when OAuth credentials exist; organizations plugin planned for Studio seats (M6); zero per-MAU cost |

R-18 dissolved Inngest's original rationale (it was Vercel-bound), and nothing in M1 needs a runner for correctness — grace/downgrade derive lazily at read time, expiry materializes in the fold, auto-top-up is request-time — so **M1 shipped runner-free by design**. The choice (Inngest vs a self-hosted alternative) is settled at **M4 entry**, where trend refresh first genuinely needs a scheduler; the M4 plan's dependency check must show a recorded decision before planning it. Deploy shape decided with the Lightsail runbook (R-18) |

60-
61-Table notes (only the non-obvious):
62-
63:- **brain_docs**: `(profile_id, kind, version, content jsonb, source_evidence jsonb, status)` - append-only versions; active = max version with `status='active'`. Editing creates a new version (REQ-B02, REQ-C05). `kind='voice'|'strategy'|'performance_meta'|'killtest'`.
64-- **generations**: `(profile_id, mode, input jsonb, output jsonb, parent_id nullable, framework_ids uuid[], trend_item_id nullable, prompt_bundle_version, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, credit_cost, kill_test jsonb, status)`. `parent_id` gives revision lineage (REQ-C06). `prompt_bundle_version` satisfies REQ-J02.
65:- **credit_ledger**: `(workspace_id, delta int, kind 'grant'|'pack'|'debit'|'refund'|'adjust'|'expiry', ref_type, ref_id, expires_at nullable, stripe_event_id nullable unique)` - append-only; **balance is a chronological lot-allocation fold over the rows, not `sum(delta)` of unexpired rows** (**D-M1-7**, recorded as R-20; this wording supersedes the original naive-sum sentence). The naive sum over-subtracts as soon as an expired grant was only partially consumed, because debits never expire: the debit stays in the sum while the grant leaves it. Instead, `grant`/`pack`/`refund` and positive `adjust` rows are consumable **lots**, `debit` and negative `adjust` rows **allocate** against live lots in the D-M1-8 order, and `expiry` rows are materialization history the fold replays. When a lot crosses its (pause-shifted) expiry with a remainder, the balance authority lazily appends an `expiry` row for it - idempotent per lot, keyed to the DB clock - so `sum(delta)` of ALL rows equals the fold's answer and "the ledger is the balance" stays literally true with no cron. Computed per request, never stored as a mutable balance (REQ-G04). Idempotency via unique `stripe_event_id` plus one business-object partial unique per mint path - invoice, checkout session, payment intent (REQ-G06).
66:- **results**: `(profile_id, generation_id nullable, platform, posted_at, views, metric_numerator, metric_kind, computed_per_1k, verified bool, confounders text[], notes)`. `verified=false` when reported without numbers - the UI stores the claim but excludes it from learning (REQ-F02).
67-- **frameworks**: `(name, slug, beats jsonb, why_it_converts text, applicability jsonb, confidence, saturation 'observed'|'emerging'|'established'|'saturated'|'retired', visibility 'shared'|'private', owner_profile_id nullable, curator_status 'proposed'|'approved'|'rejected', version)`.
68-- **trend_items**: `(source_id, external_ref, url, title, channel_ref, channel_baseline jsonb, stats jsonb, outlier_ratio numeric, observed_at, stale_after, niche_tags text[])`.
69-- **autopsies**: `(trend_item_id unique, transcript text nullable, hook_mechanic, beats jsonb, ending_style, follow_trigger, matched_framework_id nullable, proposed_framework jsonb nullable, model, version)` - cached once, served to all (REQ-E03).
70:- **promotion_proposals**: `(profile_id, target_doc kind, proposed_change jsonb, evidence jsonb {n, effect, confidence, result_ids}, status 'pending'|'accepted'|'rejected')` (REQ-F03, REQ-C05).
71-
72-## 3. The Generation Pipeline (packages/modes)
--
74-Every mode runs the same skeleton:
75-
76:1. **Assemble context** (`packages/llm/assemble.ts`): universal laws (from config, versioned) + relevant shared frameworks (retrieved by mode + niche + goal, saturated ones flagged, retired excluded) + the profile's four active brain docs + mode template + user input. The assembled bundle hash is recorded as `prompt_bundle_version`.
77-2. **Generate** on the mode's model tier (default: generation on Sonnet-class, classification/autopsy on Haiku-class; tiers in config).
78-3. **Kill test pass**: a second, cheap model call scores the draft against the profile's KillTest items; hard-rule violations (fragment triads, antithesis constructions, invented specifics without `[check]`, hook >14 words where the rule is active) trigger one automatic rewrite, then surface honestly if still failing ("everything died, here is why, here is a sharper angle to try"). Kill-test results stored on the generation (REQ-C03).
79-4. **Similarity gate** (spin only): output vs source transcript, n-gram overlap + embedding similarity thresholds from config; failure triggers rewrite, never display (REQ-E04, REQ-I02).
80:5. **Meter**: debit ledger with the operation's configured cost inside the same transaction that persists the generation; insufficient balance rejects before step 2 with the top-up prompt (REQ-G03).
81-6. **Emit** the structured output (Zod schema `ScriptOutput`: thesis, framework, hooks[], script_beats[] with timestamps and `turn` marker, shot_map[], text_on_screen, caption, why_this_performs including `weakest_point`).
82-
--
92-Explicitly not built: any adapter that scrapes TikTok/Instagram. A third adapter slot exists for a licensed data provider or official trend surface, decided post-pilot (PRD open decision 2).
93-
94:**Autopsy pipeline** (Inngest durable function): new trend_item → fetch transcript → Haiku-class autopsy in the fixed order (hook mechanic → beats → ending → follow trigger) → embed → match against framework library (embedding + LLM confirm) → cache. Unmatched strong mechanisms create a `proposed_framework` into the curation queue (REQ-D03).
95-
96-**Feed query**: per profile = tracked niches ∩ non-stale items, ranked by outlier_ratio × recency decay, saturation labels rendered (REQ-E06). Weekly digest email per profile via Inngest cron + Resend.
--
99-
100-- Stripe objects: 1 product, 4 recurring prices (free tier = no Stripe subscription, just default state); 1 one-off price for the 1,000-credit pack. Checkout Sessions for subscribe and packs; Customer Portal for everything else.
101:- Webhooks handled (single `/api/stripe/webhook`, signature-verified, idempotent on event id): `checkout.session.completed`, `customer.subscription.created|updated|deleted`, `invoice.paid` (monthly grant: insert `grant` row with `expires_at = period_end + 1 month` for rollover semantics per REQ-G02), `invoice.payment_failed` (grace state; downgrade job after 7 days), pack purchase → `pack` row, 12-month expiry.
102:- Debit order (**D-M1-8**, recorded as R-20; this wording supersedes the original "oldest unexpired first"): **soonest effective expiry first**; equal expiry -> older `created_at` first; still equal -> grants before packs; never-expiring `adjust` lots last. "Effective" means pause-shifted (R-12: a pause suspends expiry clocks). Plain oldest-first contradicted REQ-G03's "packs are consumed after monthly credits" in the ordinary case - a January pack (12-month validity) is *older* than February's grant (1-month validity), so oldest-first would burn the pack while the grant expired unused. Soonest-expiry-first satisfies both documents in every case and is the order the customer would choose. Auto-top-up: optional saved payment method + monthly cap (in cents) stored per workspace; triggered when balance < cost of the requested operation.
103:- Config (`packages/config`): credit costs per operation, tier allowances, model tiers, similarity thresholds - stored in DB with a version row, editable from admin, no deploy needed (REQ-G05). Every generation records the config version it ran under.
104:- Margin dashboard: weekly Inngest job aggregates `tokens_in/out × provider price` vs credits consumed × effective $/credit per tier → `/admin/margin` (REQ-G05).
105-
106-## 6. Auth, Tenancy, and Security
107-
108-- Server-layer session gate (R-19): `getSessionUser`/`requireAdmin` called in layouts **and** every protected/admin page; middleware performs only an optimistic session-cookie redirect (UX fast path, never the gate — Better Auth cannot verify sessions in edge middleware). Admin gated by the fail-closed `ADMIN_USER_IDS` allowlist.
109:- Every query is workspace-scoped through a single `withWorkspace(ctx)` helper; no raw table access from route handlers. Profile isolation (REQ-A03) is enforced by query scoping + a test suite that attempts cross-profile reads.
110-- Rate limits: per-user generation concurrency 2 (Free/Creator) / 4 (Pro) / 8 (Studio); IP-based limits on the public demo (REQ-H02).
111-- Secrets in server env files (local `.env`, Lightsail environment — never committed); Stripe webhook secret verified; no LLM keys client-side, ever.
112:- PII: brain docs and generations are the sensitive surface; encryption at rest is an owner obligation on the self-hosted Postgres (R-18 — RUNBOOK item at first deploy), export and deletion flows per REQ-A04.

64-## Standing risks (watch from M0)
65-
66:1. **Margin inversion at Pro/Studio heavy use** - the margin dashboard exists from M1's config and M6's rollup precisely so pricing is tuned from data; credit costs are config, not code.
67-2. **The similarity gate under-blocking** - keep a growing fixture set of near-copies; every gate change reruns it.
68-3. **Trend source fragility** - the YouTube adapter is quota-bound and ToS-bound; the `TrendSource` interface exists so a licensed provider can slot in without touching the pipeline.
69:4. **Brain quality at onboarding** - a thin brain produces generic output, which is the product's one unforgivable sin; M3's evidence criterion and the pilot phase are the honest checks, and REQ-B04's first-three-ideas moment is the earliest signal.

19-## R-3: Spin, never copy (2026-08-13)
20-
21:**Context:** Owner asked for a trend monitor that lets creators "copy" trending posts. Platforms deprioritise or de-recommend unoriginal content; the product's own corpus evidence shows adapted mechanisms outperform copies; verbatim reproduction is also a rights risk.
22-**Decision:** The feature is capture → autopsy → Spin (mechanism kept, subject/wording/structure changed, similarity-gated). Verbatim or near-verbatim output is a hard release gate (REQ-E04/I02). The user-facing framing: "make my version".
23-**Consequences:** Slightly more model spend per trend action (autopsy cached to offset); a defensible feature that survives platform policy enforcement.

51-**Consequences:** Portability (export works), inspectability (creator sees exactly what the system believes), and provider independence.

125:## R-20: M1 billing defaults — idempotency, config, pause, balance fold, consumption order (2026-08-14)
126-
127:**Context:** M1 (billing + credit ledger) needed eight defaults the doc set didn't settle. Chosen per the build-plan working agreement (most reversible default, recorded, revisit trigger) and hardened through the M1 plan-review gate (Codex + billing×2 + tenancy×2 + generalist; `docs/progress/respin-m1-plan-review.md`).
128-
129-**Decisions:**
130:- **D-M1-1 — Webhook idempotency:** dedicated `stripe_events` table (Stripe event id PK, `workspace_id`/`stripe_customer_id` resolved at receipt, **`received_at`/`processed_at` in place of the house `created_at`/`updated_at` pair** — rows commit once under the single-tx design, so an `updated_at` would be a lie; the named deviation from tech-spec §2's all-tables rule) + the ledger's unique `stripe_event_id` as defense-in-depth. Single-transaction dispatch: event-row insert + handler + processed-mark commit together; failure rolls the row back so an existing row always means final; never early-200 on in-flight work. *Revisit: never on principle.*
131:- **D-M1-2 — Config versioning:** append-only `config_versions` rows (integer identity, jsonb content, author); active = max version; Zod-validated. *Revisit: per-key versioning only if whole-document churn gets noisy.*
132:- **D-M1-3 — Pause representation:** ledger rows immutable; `pause_periods` one row per pause (close-on-resume sets `ended_at` — its ONE sanctioned update; the table is not append-only); effective expiry computed derivation-time by pause-overlap fold. *Revisit: shift-on-resume UPDATE + audit row if fold cost bites.*
133:- **D-M1-4 — No job runner at M1:** grace/downgrade derived lazily from webhook facts + clock; Stripe dunning drives eventual cancellation; auto-top-up is request-time (`maybeAutoTopup` ships and is tested at M1; the debit-refusal call site is M3's); expiry is derivation-time. *Revisit: M4 /create-plan entry — trend refresh needs a scheduler; the M4 plan must show a recorded runner decision.*
134:- **D-M1-5 — Email dual-truth:** `users.email` dropped; Better Auth `user.email` is the sole email truth, read from the session (the FK is a constraint, not a licence to join). Structurally retires the M0 empty-email-guard deferral. New FK `users.auth_user_id → user.id` ON DELETE RESTRICT (M6 deletion must remove both sides explicitly). *Revisit: only if a domain-side email cache is ever needed.*
135:- **D-M1-6 — Stripe→workspace resolution:** stored `stripe_customer_id → workspace` mapping (created at checkout creation) is the sole authority; Checkout metadata is a cross-check; unknown customer / null customer field / mismatch ⇒ recorded refusal (`refused_unknown_customer` / `refused_identity_mismatch`), 200, zero ledger writes; refusal logs carry **ids, never payload fields** — event id, outcome, and the Stripe object id concerned; never email/name/address/amount and never the payload object (round-7 wording correction: the operative invariant is ids-not-PII, and the object id is what makes a refusal diagnosable). *Revisit: never on principle.*
136:- **D-M1-7 — Balance derivation:** chronological lot-allocation fold over all six kinds (`grant`/`pack`/`refund` + positive `adjust` are lots; `debit` + negative `adjust` allocate; `expiry` rows are replayed as history, never recomputed); lazy `expiry` materialization idempotent per lot, keyed to DB `now()` (caller `at` = pure read; allocating writes reject skewed/retroactive `at`); joins a caller tx that already holds the per-workspace advisory lock, opens its own locked tx on the bare-db path. A refund inherits the latest effective expiry of the lots its debit consumed — a refund of expired credits is born expired (goodwill = admin `adjust` with explicit expiry). Invariant: post-materialization `sum(delta)` of ALL rows equals the fold. Supersedes tech-spec §2's naive "sum of unexpired rows" wording (sync in M1 phase 4). *Revisit: snapshot rows if fold cost bites — never a mutable counter.*
137:- **D-M1-8 — Lot consumption order:** soonest effective expiry first; equal → older first; then grants before packs; never-expiring `adjust` lots last. Resolves REQ-G03 ("packs after monthly credits") vs tech-spec §5 ("oldest first"): a January pack is older than February's grant, so plain oldest-first burns the 12-month pack while the 1-month grant expires — soonest-expiry-first satisfies both documents in every case (sync §5 in M1 phase 4). Stated consequence (plan-review F2): mid-cycle upgrades grant no extra allowance until the next billing anniversary (REQ-G02's anniversary reset). *Revisit: never on principle.*
138-
139:**Consequences:** the ledger stays literally equal to its sum; webhook handling is replay-safe by construction; M1 ships with zero background infrastructure; the auth/domain identity model is provider-neutral with fail-closed deletion.
140-
141-## R-21: Free-tier credits have no minting path until M3 (2026-08-16)
142-
143:**Context:** M1 phase 3's billing gate (round 7, CHANGE 5) grepped every consumer of the seeded config key `allowances.free = 25` and found exactly one: the `invoice.paid` webhook handler. A Free workspace has **no Stripe subscription** by design (skill B6, R-7: Free is the absence of a subscription, not a $0 price) and therefore never produces an invoice — so nothing in the shipped system can ever mint the 25 monthly credits PRD §4G promises. It was an *unnamed gap*: no Deferral Ledger row, no build-plan M1 accept-when, no decision entry — the shape this repo has repeatedly recorded as how "present-and-unrun" becomes "recorded as done".
144-
145:**Decision:** Name it as a deferral rather than build a minting mechanism inside M1 phase 3 (which is Stripe-integration scope and would be unplanned work on the money path). **Stated consequence, plainly: until M3, a Free workspace has a zero credit balance and can generate nothing.** The receiver is **build-plan M3**, at the credit-debit call site — the same place tier gating ships, and the only place a derivation-time mint can live given D-M1-4's "no background job runner at M1" (an expiring monthly free grant, minted lazily and idempotently per workspace per calendar month, is the shape that fits; a cron is excluded by D-M1-4 until the M4 runner decision).
146-
147-**Tripwire:** the M3 plan's Stop-Condition-2 dependency check must clear the master-plan Deferral Ledger row "Free-tier monthly allowance has no minting path" by showing EITHER a free-allowance minting design at the debit site (with its idempotency key) OR a recorded decision that Free ships with zero credits, with PRD §4G corrected in the same change. `allowances.free` stays in config v1 meanwhile: it is the number the eventual mint will read, and removing it would hide the gap rather than close it.

151-## R-22: Cancellation stays available in Stripe's Customer Portal (2026-08-17)
152-
153:**Context:** REQ-G08 / billing skill B4 require that the cancel flow **always offers pause first**. Respin has no in-app cancellation API at M1 — the in-app path is `/settings/billing` → "Cancel subscription" → an interstitial that offers pause **above** the way out, and the way out is a link into Stripe's Customer Portal, which is where the cancellation actually happens (asserted by the AC-3 DOM-order test and its `data-cancel="final"` marker). M1 phase 4's round-2 billing gate pointed out that the same portal is reachable from two other controls that carry no pause offer (the "Manage plan and payment method" button on a live subscription, and the portal button on `/usage`), and from Stripe's own emails — so the pause-first rule was resting on a Stripe **dashboard configuration nobody had written down**: whether the portal's `subscription_cancel` feature is on.
154-
155:**Decision:** **Portal cancellation stays enabled**, and that is recorded here rather than left to a default. Disabling it would (a) break the documented evidence step that cancels through the portal, (b) leave a subscriber with no self-serve way out of a paid subscription — a worse outcome than an un-offered pause, and a poor one to defend to a consumer-protection regulator — and (c) not even close the hole, since Stripe emails link to the portal directly. What REQ-G08 binds is **Respin's own cancel flow**, and that is enforced mechanically where we control it.
156-
157:**Consequence, stated plainly:** a creator who reaches the Customer Portal by any route other than our interstitial can cancel without ever being offered a pause. The pause offer is a *product* control on our surface, not a *guarantee* about Stripe's.
158-
159:**Compensating control (runbook, not code):** the README's Stripe setup gains a step that makes the operator **look at** the portal's feature configuration and record what it says. Verified against the installed SDK (`stripe@22.5.0`, golden rule 9): `BillingPortal.Configurations` carries a `subscription_cancel` feature and **no `subscription_pause` feature at all** — so the portal cannot be made to offer our pause even in principle, which is why the answer here is "record the choice", not "configure it away". A dashboard setting that no step names is exactly the kind of unwritten dependency this doc set exists to stop.
160-
161:**Revisit:** when an in-app cancellation API ships (which would let the interstitial complete the cancellation itself, making the portal route optional), or if pilot data shows portal cancellations materially outnumber interstitial ones — at which point the win-back/pause offer belongs in the M6 email flow instead.
162-
163-## R-23: Correction to R-22's third reason (append-only, 2026-08-17)
--
165-**This entry corrects R-22 above; R-22 is left as written because this file is append-only.**
166-
167:**What is wrong:** R-22's decision paragraph gives three reasons for leaving portal cancellation enabled, and reason **(c)** — "and not even close the hole, since Stripe emails link to the portal directly" — is **not accurate**. A Customer Portal session renders the features its configuration enables. With `subscription_cancel` disabled, the emailed portal link opens a portal that shows **no cancellation control at all**; the email is a route *to the portal*, not a route *around its configuration*. So disabling the feature genuinely WOULD close the hole R-22 describes. Found by the M1 phase-4 round-3 billing gate.
168-
169:**What is unchanged:** the decision itself. Reasons **(a)** (disabling breaks the documented evidence step that cancels through the portal) and **(b)** (it leaves a paying subscriber with no self-serve exit — the worse outcome, and the harder one to defend to a consumer-protection regulator) stand on their own and are sufficient. R-22's SDK claim is also unchanged and was independently verified: `stripe@22.5.0`'s `BillingPortal.Configurations` carries a `subscription_cancel` feature and no `subscription_pause` feature at all.
170-
171:**Why this is worth an entry rather than a silent edit:** an overstated argument is a decision that looks better supported than it is, and the next person to weigh "should we disable portal cancellation?" would have read reason (c) as settling a question it does not settle. The honest statement is: **we could close this hole and are choosing not to, for reasons (a) and (b).**
172-
173:**Revisit:** unchanged from R-22 — when an in-app cancellation API ships, or if pilot data shows portal cancellations materially outnumber interstitial ones.

175-## R-24: `CLOCK_SKEW_MS` is one 60-second tolerance doing three jobs (2026-08-17)
176-
177:**Context:** `packages/credits/src/clock.ts` exports `CLOCK_SKEW_MS = 60_000`. It was introduced for ONE job — the allocating-write clock guard, where it means "a caller's `at` more than a minute from the database clock is a stale clock, not an ordering artefact" (D-M1-7, tenancy code-review BLOCK 1). It has since acquired two more, both on the pause bounds in `pause.ts`: the OPEN-side staleness bound (round 8 / migration 0007) and the CLOSE-side one (round 8 / round-3 migration 0008). In those two it is not a clock-skew tolerance at all — it is a **webhook delivery-lag / granularity tolerance**: Stripe's `event.created` is second-granularity while our stored instants are the millisecond DB clock, so an ordinary reconciling snapshot is routinely a few hundred milliseconds "older" than the row it reconciles. The billing gate's round-3 NOTE is correct that this threshold had **no PRD or decision citation** (skill B5, threshold provenance) — a comment is not provenance.
178-
179-**Decision:** record the threshold **here** rather than move it into `packages/config`, and keep the single constant.
180-
181:- Against a config key: `pause.ts` takes no config today, so threading one in means changing `ensurePauseStarted`/`ensurePauseEnded`'s signatures and both call sites, plus a config read inside the webhook transaction — new work on the money path, inside a fix round, for a number nobody has yet had a reason to change. This repo's own record (five of eight M1 rounds shipped a defect inside their own fix) is the argument against.
182-- Against splitting it into two constants: there is no measurement distinguishing them. Inventing `WEBHOOK_LAG_TOLERANCE_MS = 60_000` beside `CLOCK_SKEW_MS = 60_000` would look like two calibrated numbers where there is one guess.
183-
184:**What the number actually claims, stated plainly:** 60 seconds is a *guess* chosen to be comfortably larger than second-level rounding and same-second races, and comfortably smaller than the minutes-to-hours staleness the bounds exist to refuse. It is **not** measured against real Stripe delivery lag. Its failure mode is bounded and known in both directions: too small refuses a legitimate reconciling snapshot (the pause converges on the next event, or on the owner's own action); too large lets a snapshot up to a minute stale act (bounded, and both bounds are additionally protected by the `mirrorEventAt` order guard).
185-
186:**Tripwire / revisit:** the M1 owner evidence run (`stripe listen`, the run that closes E1–E8) is the first time real `event.created` → processing lag is observable. Record the observed lag in the ledger during that run. If any legitimate event's lag exceeds ~30s, or if a pause/resume is refused during it, split the constant and give the delivery-lag half a config key with the measured value. Also revisit if M4's background-job runner introduces queued (rather than inline) webhook processing, which would raise lag by construction.

  109:   it(
  110:     "ROUND 7 (B1/B3): a debit CANNOT ignore a debit that committed after its own transaction began â€” `now()` is the transaction's start, not the clock",
  111:     { timeout: 60_000 },
  112:     async () => {
  113:       // THE DETERMINISTIC FORM of the intermittent "11 of 20 concurrent debits
  114:       // of 10 succeeded against a 100 balance" failure. Round 6 read that
  115:       // symptom as suite interference and gave each Docker suite its own
  116:       // database; the symptom survived (2 of 5 standalone runs of this file,
  117:       // with no neighbour that could reset anything), because the real cause is
  118:       // in the balance authority:
  119:       //
  120:       //   `getDbNow` ran `SELECT now()`, and in PostgreSQL `now()` is
  121:       //   `transaction_timestamp()` â€” fixed at the START of the calling
  122:       //   transaction. `foldLedger` then drops every row whose `created_at` is
  123:       //   later than that `asOf`. A debit row written by a transaction that
  124:       //   BEGAN after mine but COMMITTED before I took the workspace lock is
  125:       //   therefore invisible to my fold: I see a balance that has already been
  126:       //   spent, and B3's "refuse before writing" check passes on it.
  127:       //
  128:       // The race above only reproduces it when the 20 BEGINs happen to overlap
  129:       // the right way. This case forces the interleaving, so it fails EVERY run
  130:       // against `now()` and passes every run against `clock_timestamp()`.
  131:       const { db } = harness;
  132:       const ws = await mkWorkspace();
  133:       await db.transaction((t) =>
  134:         grantCredits(t, {
  135:           workspaceId: ws, amount: 100,
  136:           expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 24 * HOUR),
  137:           refType: "invoice", refId: "in_txstart_race", configVersion: 1,
  138:         })
  139:       );
  140: 
  141:       let releaseB: () => void = () => {};
  142:       const bMayRun = new Promise<void>((r) => {
  143:         releaseB = r;
  144:       });
  145:       let bDone: Promise<unknown> = Promise.resolve();
  146: 
  147:       const aResult = await db
  148:         .transaction(async (tx) => {
  149:           // Pin A's transaction_timestamp BEFORE B exists, and take no lock.
  150:           await tx.execute(sql`SELECT 1`);
  151:           // Now let B spend the whole balance on another connection and commit.
  152:           bDone = db.transaction((t2) =>
  153:             debitCredits(t2, {
  154:               workspaceId: ws, cost: 100, refType: "race", refId: "b_spends_all",
  155:               at: new Date(), configVersion: 1,
  156:             })
  157:           );
  158:           releaseB();
  159:           await bDone;
  160:           // A's debit runs strictly AFTER B committed. It must see B's row.
  161:           return debitCredits(tx, {
  162:             workspaceId: ws, cost: 10, refType: "race", refId: "a_after_b",
  163:             at: new Date(), configVersion: 1,
  164:           });
  165:         })
  166:         .then(
  167:           (row) => ({ ok: true as const, row }),
  168:           (err: unknown) => ({ ok: false as const, err })
  169:         );
  170:       await bMayRun;
  171:       await bDone.catch(() => undefined);
  172: 
  173:       expect(
  174:         aResult.ok,
  175:         "A debited a balance B had already spent â€” the ledger over-consumed"
  176:       ).toBe(false);
  177:       expect(
  178:         aResult.ok ? null : aResult.err,
  179:         "and it must be the ordinary typed refusal, not some other failure"
  180:       ).toBeInstanceOf(InsufficientCreditsError);
  181:       // B1: the ledger is the balance, and it never went negative.
  182:       const rows = (await db.select().from(creditLedger)).filter(
  183:         (r) => r.workspaceId === ws
  184:       );
  185:       expect(rows.reduce((s, r) => s + r.delta, 0)).toBe(0);
  186:       expect((await deriveBalance(db, ws)).balance).toBe(0);
  187:     }
  188:   );

  190:   it(
  191:     "ROUND 10 (write clock): a GRANT that commits while a debit's transaction is open must sort BEFORE that debit â€” deriveBalance keeps folding forever after",
  192:     { timeout: 60_000 },
  193:     async () => {
  194:       // THE MIRROR IMAGE of the ROUND 7 case above. That one constructs this
  195:       // exact interleaving in the DEBIT direction, where the right outcome is a
  196:       // refusal â€” so it proved the READ clock and said nothing about the WRITE
  197:       // clock. Here B GRANTS instead of spending, so the debit is correctly
  198:       // ALLOWED, and the question becomes what instant its row is dated at.
  199:       //
  200:       //   A BEGINs at t0. B grants 100 and commits at t1 > t0. A folds at t2
  201:       //   (clock_timestamp), SEES the grant, and debits 10 â€” correctly. With the
  202:       //   column default that row is written at `now()` = transaction_timestamp
  203:       //   = t0, i.e. BEFORE the grant that funded it. Every later fold then
  204:       //   replays debit-then-grant, finds no live lot, and throws
  205:       //   LedgerIntegrityError "over-consumes" â€” PERMANENTLY, because
  206:       //   credit_ledger is append-only and the row cannot be removed. The
  207:       //   workspace loses its usage page, every future debit and every refund,
  208:       //   while webhook grants keep landing and the customer keeps paying.
  209:       //
  210:       // So the assertion is not "the debit is refused" but "the ledger is still
  211:       // readable" â€” deriveBalance must FOLD, not throw.
  212:       const { db } = harness;
  213:       const ws = await mkWorkspace();
  214: 
  215:       let bDone: Promise<unknown> = Promise.resolve();
  216:       const aResult = await db
  217:         .transaction(async (tx) => {
  218:           // Pin A's transaction_timestamp BEFORE B exists, and take no lock.
  219:           await tx.execute(sql`SELECT 1`);
  220:           await tx.execute(sql`SELECT pg_sleep(0.05)`);
  221:           // B grants on another connection and commits.
  222:           bDone = db.transaction((t2) =>
  223:             grantCredits(t2, {
  224:               workspaceId: ws, amount: 100,
  225:               expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 24 * HOUR),
  226:               refType: "invoice", refId: "in_write_clock", configVersion: 1,
  227:             })
  228:           );
  229:           await bDone;
  230:           // A's debit runs strictly AFTER B committed and is FUNDED by it.
  231:           return debitCredits(tx, {
  232:             workspaceId: ws, cost: 10, refType: "race", refId: "a_funded_by_b",
  233:             at: new Date(), configVersion: 1,
  234:           });
  235:         })
  236:         .then(
  237:           (row) => ({ ok: true as const, row }),
  238:           (err: unknown) => ({ ok: false as const, err })
  239:         );
  240:       await bDone.catch(() => undefined);
  241: 
  242:       expect(
  243:         aResult.ok ? null : aResult.err,
  244:         "the debit is funded by a grant the fold can see â€” it must succeed"
  245:       ).toBeNull();
  246: 
  247:       // THE DISCRIMINATOR: the row must be dated at or after the grant that
  248:       // funded it, so the chronological fold can replay it.
  249:       const rows = (await db.select().from(creditLedger)).filter(
  250:         (r) => r.workspaceId === ws
  251:       );
  252:       const grant = rows.find((r) => r.kind === "grant")!;
  253:       const debit = rows.find((r) => r.kind === "debit")!;
  254:       expect(
  255:         debit.createdAt.getTime(),
  256:         `debit dated ${debit.createdAt.toISOString()} but the grant funding it is dated ${grant.createdAt.toISOString()} â€” the ledger now folds to an integrity error that can never be repaired`
  257:       ).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(grant.createdAt.getTime());
  258: 
  259:       // ...stated as the consequence, not just the cause: the balance authority
  260:       // still answers, now and on every future read.
  261:       const view = await deriveBalance(db, ws);
  262:       expect(view.balance).toBe(90);
  263:       expect(rows.reduce((s, r) => s + r.delta, 0)).toBe(90);
  264:       // A second read (the usage page after a refresh) must also survive.
  265:       expect((await deriveBalance(db, ws)).balance).toBe(90);
  266:     }
  267:   );

   37: /**
   38:  * Fixture type pressure (code-review CHANGE, and the ROOT CAUSE of blockers 1
   39:  * and 3): every fixture below is checked against the INSTALLED SDK's own types
   40:  * via `satisfies DeepPartial<T>`. A field that does not exist on the real
   41:  * Stripe object â€” the fabricated `customer` on a Customer that hid blocker 1 â€”
   42:  * or one with the wrong value type is now a red typecheck, not a green test.
   43:  *
   44:  * DeepPartial (not Partial) keeps fixtures small without losing that check at
   45:  * nested levels, where both blockers actually lived (`invoice.lines[].period`,
   46:  * `session.payment_status`). Required fields we deliberately omit are not the
   47:  * defect class these tests exist to catch; MISNAMED and MIS-TYPED ones are.
   48:  *
   49:  * KNOWN LIMITS â€” do not over-trust this guard (code-review NOTE):
   50:  *  1. An OMITTED field is invisible, by construction.
   51:  *  2. Stripe widens many unions with `OtherString` (= string & {}), so a wrong
   52:  *     VALUE on those still compiles: `payment_status: "settled"` type-checks.
   53:  *     `billing_reason` has no OtherString, which is why the untyped one there
   54:  *     was caught.
   55:  *  3. It is a SHAPE check, not a semantics check. It could not have caught
   56:  *     reading the wrong invoice LINE â€” that defect needed a fixture with two
   57:  *     lines and a test that asserts which one was used.
   58:  */
   59: type DeepPartial<T> = T extends (infer U)[]
   60:   ? DeepPartial<U>[]
   61:   : T extends object
   62:     ? { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> }
   63:     : T;
   64:

   71:  * already been applied to `object` by its builder before it arrives here.

codex
- [P1] `respin/packages/credits/src/stripe/webhooks.ts:451-459,520-563,604-636` — The mirror watermark is checked before an unconditional workspace-wide update. Concurrent Stripe events can both read the old watermark; a stale event can then overwrite a newer subscription state, including resurrecting a cancellation or restoring stale price/cancellation data.

- [P1] `respin/packages/credits/src/stripe/webhooks.ts:195-197,658-789,814-847` — Invoice events are scoped only by customer, not subscription ID. After resubscription, a paid or failed invoice from the old subscription can grant credits to the new workspace or put the new subscription into dunning.

- [P1] `respin/packages/config/src/schema.ts:29-35`, `respin/packages/credits/src/stripe/actions.ts:284-291`, `respin/packages/credits/src/stripe/auto-topup.ts:85-128` — Manual packs charge Stripe’s immutable price, while auto-top-ups charge editable `config.pack.priceUsd`. The setup script detects divergence only when manually rerun; an admin config change immediately creates two prices for the same credits and misstates the manual checkout price.

- [P1] `respin/packages/credits/src/state.ts:39-46,134-152`, `respin/app/(product)/settings/billing/page.tsx:61-63`, `respin/app/(product)/settings/billing/billing-view.tsx:261-280` — `incomplete` subscriptions count as live for duplicate-checkout prevention but render as Free. The UI hides Subscribe and offers the Customer Portal, which cannot resolve an incomplete subscription; a failed/SCA-required first payment leaves the customer without an actionable recovery path.

- [P1] `respin/packages/credits/src/stripe/webhooks.ts:139-148,621-636`, `respin/packages/credits/src/state.ts:104-149` — Dead-subscription cleanup does not clear `pausedAt` or `resumesAt`, and billing state checks `pausedAt` before terminal status. If the pause mirror and pause-period history drift, cancellation can leave the workspace rendering as paused and still resolving a paid tier.

- [P1] `docs/initial/PRD.md:118`, `respin/packages/credits/src/stripe/webhooks.ts:640-641`, `respin/packages/credits/tests/stripe.test.ts:630-641` — The PRD promises “no monthly grants” while paused, but the handler deliberately processes `invoice.paid` and grants the allowance while paused. The test locks in behavior contrary to the product requirement.

- [P2] `respin/packages/credits/src/stripe/webhooks.ts:40-45,337-343,745-778,287-307` — Concurrent deliveries of the same Checkout session or invoice under different event IDs can lose on the business-object unique index and return 500. The event is retried rather than converging directly to `ignored`, producing avoidable Stripe retry/error noise.

- [P2] `respin/packages/credits/src/stripe/webhooks.ts:493-499,520-563` — Subscription snapshots with zero items are accepted. The code writes an active subscription with a null price, causing a paying workspace to become Free while still being blocked from starting another checkout.

- [P2] `respin/app/(product)/settings/billing/billing-view.tsx:342-391`, `respin/README.md:86-89` — The keyless-install promise says every billing control is disabled with a remedy, but the auto-top-up form ignores the missing Stripe/config guards and can still arm the local auto-top-up flag.
